In accordance with the principle of superposition, the solution for a particle's off-center circular orbit with random forces can be derived from the combination of random forces and the solution for a particle in a stable, central force field. This paper focuses on the particle's response to the random forces, specifically the magnitude of its angular displacement and the force acting on it, both of which are dependent on position and time. Additionally, the random nature of the final angular displacement when subjected to random forces is discussed, along with its distribution and an explicit formula for the associated probability density function.

This research focuses on fractional Sobolev spaces on compact Riemannian manifolds with inhomogeneous dimensions, and constructs a single, unified invariant Sobolev norm that encompasses all fractional indices. Through this, we derive sharp fractional Sobolev inequalities with sharp constants and no free parameters for the indicated norms. Furthermore, we establish the existence of fractional Hardy inequalities with optimal constants, under the condition that the function's integral of the absolute value over the entire manifold tends to a value other than zero or infinity as relevant.

This research explores the development of multi-trajectory particle smoothers, which maintain trajectory-level diversity while incorporating sequential estimation techniques to minimize the variance of object counts in a fixed reference frame. A key innovation is a novel resampling method that simultaneously optimizes both trajectory diversity and object count variance. This approach is challenging due to the necessity of evaluating the joint probability of particle weights and object counts before and after observation. To overcome this issue, we employ a novel method to approximate the conditional weight distribution of trajectories. This approximation is based on the assumption that the object count is conditionally independent of past observations, given the distance between objects. This assumption is valid in scenarios where the observation model is a function of object counts, such as in a Gaussian observation model. Our approach is demonstrated through simulations in Gaussian and observation-only scenarios, revealing its potential to outperform existing particle smoothers, although further performance enhancements are possible by incorporating additional observation models.

The rapid expansion of renewable energy sources and power electronics converters has led to concerns regarding their impact on stable operation of the electrical grid, particularly due to resonance and oscillations at high frequencies. To address this issue, research has focused on developing an innovative control approach leveraging positive order system-based control (PTSSC) methods. By applying PTSSC to a power system, it can effectively dampen electrical oscillations at a local level, ensuring the system remains stable under external disturbances. The approach relies on a reduced-order model of the system, which accurately captures its behavior and allows for the implementation of control algorithms. The PTSSC method is applied through a passive approach, which can be easily implemented in physical terms. The effectiveness of the PTSSC method is demonstrated through a series of simulation studies utilizing the IEEE-39-bus system and a single-machine-unloaded system, showcasing its ability to effectively dampen local oscillations.

This research paper introduces three indices to represent the offline signature templates, based on their distinct characteristics, including the signature's clarity, localization, and overall signature cycle. We applied these signatures to our unique, online learning handwriting signature recognition system, which relies on a two-stage approach, initially leveraging a deep neural network to predict the signature's location and then employing a convolutional neural network to determine the signature's shape. By utilizing these signatures in our model, we were able to achieve an accuracy rate of 97.59% on the TMC 2008 signature verification dataset.

This study examines the lattice point count within a triangle ABC with coordinates derived from a given basis in a lattice. It is well established that for triangles with vertex coordinates based on integer values, the count equals a polynomial of the triangle's vertices evaluated at (1,1,1). Building on this concept, for lattices defined by either unimodular or Euclidean bases, the count equals a polynomial of the triangle's vertices evaluated at specific basis values. These results are further applied to 3-4-5 triangles, yielding closed forms for their lattice point counts.

Context-awareness is crucial for mobile applications, but developing mobile context-aware components is difficult due to the need for explicit context binding that can negatively affect the application's usability. The MEC tool aims to simplify context-aware component development, enabling context adaptation via runtime configuration changes. In this paper, we demonstrate MEC's applicability to existing Android components, presenting a scalable implementation and testing it on a range of components and mobile platforms.

This paper introduces a novel attention-based method for pose estimation that incorporates spatial modeling to better address the challenges of occlusion and deformation. To achieve this, we propose a multi-layer attention mechanism that dynamically weighs the importance of local features, complemented by a global attention approach that captures global pose information. Furthermore, we incorporate a global model into our network to enhance the discriminative capacity of local features. Our approach yields state-of-the-art results on the COCO dataset for both pose estimation and human parsing tasks.

A novel method for measuring the astronomical energy of sources, independent of the telescope used, has been developed by recording the counts as a function of the source's position with respect to our planet. This approach involves observing the occultation of a source by the Earth and analyzing the changes in the observed counts in real-time. This innovative technique, capable of detecting sources with a sensitivity of 0.1 GHz, has been successfully tested on the radio telescope of the National Astronomical Observatory of China. By analyzing the occultation data from a blazar 3C 454.3, we demonstrated that this method can accurately determine the source's flux density. This method has the potential to be applied to a wide range of radio telescopes worldwide and can be used to conduct regular monitoring of celestial sources.

Beyond ensuring a blockchain protocol is theoretically secure, its real-world effectiveness also depends on its ability to operate without breaking down and to minimize the cost associated with adjusting protocol parameters. Achieving this requires analyzing how practical aspects like energy consumption and network communication influence the reliability and efficiency of blockchain systems. Unfortunately, current models fail to account for these critical factors. To bridge this gap, a new framework has been developed that incorporates energy consumption and network communication into the analysis of blockchain systems. This framework provides a quantitative means of evaluating the performance of blockchain protocols in a more realistic context.

Tightly bound exotic states known as tetraquarks have been proposed as potential candidates to explain various heavy states observed in experiments. Specifically, tetraquarks consisting of two heavy heavy quarks are considered prime candidates and should be thoroughly investigated. In this research, we examine the tetraquark states consisting of two heavy heavy quarks, with masses of $q\bar{q}\bar{q}\bar{q}$ and $q\bar{Q}\bar{q}\bar{Q}$, where $q$ and $Q$ can be either charm or bottom quarks. We derive the mass of these tetraquarks from the Fierz transformation of the Bethe-Salpeter equation and calculate their binding energies relative to the corresponding quark-antiquark states. Our results reveal that the tetraquarks have binding energies in the range of 0 to 20 MeV, which is consistent with the experimental data. This suggests that the tetraquarks have relatively weak binding with quarks, which is consistent with their expectation as exotic states.

We assess the connection between the long-lasting stability of the electroweak vacuum and the dynamic Higgs mass, specifically within the two Higgs doublet model of Type II. By employing a novel approach that combines the effective potential approximation and the minimization of vacuum energy, we investigate the metastability of the electroweak vacuum at both one and two-loop orders. The results show a strong correlation between the two, enabling the use of two-loop calculations to refine predictions for the Higgs mass. Furthermore, we examine the impact of explicit CP violation on vacuum metastability, providing insights into potential future studies in this area.

We establish the $q-$Logarithmic Sobolev inequality for probability measures defined in terms of Carnot-Carath\'eodory distance in Carnot group contexts, as well as in Riemannian settings with Bakry-Emery geometry, where the cost of moving within geodesic distance is proportional to the first power of the distance. Additionally, we demonstrate that this inequality can be used to derive the family of Poincar\'e inequalities with Bakry-Emery type weights for graded hypersurface groups.

A new family of estimators, distinct from the Fisher information-based maximum likelihood estimator, has been developed for location parameter estimation in skew normal distributions. This estimator is rooted in Bregman divergences and encompasses the density power divergence class, specifically yielding the density power divergence estimator as a notable instance. We have investigated the asymptotic behavior of this estimator, demonstrating its large sample distribution and determining its asymptotic design value. A comprehensive comparison with existing estimators has been conducted under a square error loss function. This comparison, along with a simulation study, helps to establish the effectiveness and superior performance of the proposed estimator. Furthermore, its real-world applicability has been exemplified through its practical application.

We propose a novel, trainable neural model capable of generating dynamic scene views by simulating light-ray transformations within complex, unstructured environments. Diverging from existing methods, our model doesn't necessitate spatial coherence, nor does it rely on predefined 3D models or structured scene representations. Utilizing a self-supervised neural radiance model, we process video data to synthesize novel views and subsequently apply a trainable volume rendering framework. This framework leverages a recurrent neural architecture to dynamically segment and transform the scene volume, effectively addressing occlusion and enabling high-resolution image synthesis. Experimental results demonstrate our model's efficacy in synthesizing realistic, dynamic scenes with intricate details, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods in both qualitative and quantitative assessments.

We study the statistical behavior of chaotic quantum graphs featuring two adjacent identical sub-graphs connected through a mixed Petermann mixing region with a mixing strength of α. The graphs are characterized by a set of natural boundary conditions defined by transmission coefficients τ1 and τ2 for the sub-graphs. We find that the eigenvalue density of the graphs exhibits a scaling phenomenon near the spectrum edge, and by deriving an effective action for the dominant orbits, we obtain the leading-order eigenvalue asymptotics. We further investigate the partial sums of eigenvalues and the Bessel moments of the eigenvalue density, and show that the partial sums exhibit a polynomial growth with a leading term of √n, where n represents the partial sum index, and that the Bessel moments exhibit a polynomial growth with a leading term of O(1) in the α strength when the graph size and eigenvalue index n approach infinity.

Variable stars hold a crucial place in understanding the universe and its evolution, and determining their orbital periods accurately is vital for building reliable star catalogs. The Gaia mission has significantly improved the number of known periodic variables, and combining its data with existing information has led to a global analysis of variable sources. Our research leverages the EDR3 dataset release, which provides the most comprehensive star catalog to date. Our analysis of 16.9 million Gaia sources identifies 7.9 million period candidates and 1.6 million period determinations, and applying a new period-luminosity relation to our data reveals that the period distribution of stars follows a power law with a slope of -2.24. Our results also show that the period distribution remains consistent across different mass ranges and types of variable sources.

Passive systems have gained significant interest in the systems and control community, particularly in the design of stable and robust controllers. This work investigates the properties of negative imaginary systems, which are a specific class of passive systems, and develop a two-degree-of-freedom controller based on their transfer matrix parameters. The stability of the closed-loop system is analyzed and conditions for ideal tracking are derived. Furthermore, it is shown that the controlled nominal nominal negative imaginary system is internally stable with a stable transfer function. Additionally, sufficient conditions for negative imaginary system order are established.

The ability of a model to learn multiple skills is known as multi-task learning, but a significant problem it poses is known as catastrophic forgetting. This phenomenon causes new skills to force erase previously acquired ones from memory. This research investigates whether a model can develop a mechanism to prevent this effect. It presents a method to avoid catastrophic forgetting in multi-task learning models, called incremental multi-task learning. By breaking down the learning process into smaller chunks and gradually increasing the difficulty level, this approach enables models to acquire new skills without losing previously learned ones. Experimental results show that this method can successfully prevent catastrophic forgetting in various neural network architectures.

In today's society, people from diverse backgrounds interact freely, often combining their languages when communicating. This phenomenon is referred to as code-switching. Current automatic speech recognition (ASR systems struggle to comprehend code-switched speech, which limits their usefulness. This study aims to improve the performance of an ASR system by fine-tuning its language model on code-switched speech. The researchers first identified the most frequently switched languages by analyzing a large dataset of spoken language. They then trained the language model using the top three language pairs - English with Spanish, English with French, and English with Portuguese. The results showed a notable improvement in language model accuracy, which ranged from 14% to 29%. The researchers also observed that their language model was able to switch languages mid-sentence more accurately.

This lecture will cover three unresolved topics in particle physics and cosmology, all seeking answers to what comprises regular matter, dark matter, and what drives dark energy within the universe.  It will examine the potential interplay between the dark sector and quantum field theory, the breakdown of $SU(2)_W$ symmetry due to the dark sector, and how the dark sector influences the properties of regular matter.  Our current understanding of regular matter will serve as a springboard for an exploration of these mysteries.

Predicting how well users respond to specific online application features is crucial for understanding user preferences and tailoring the user experience accordingly. Existing models that rely on feature-based representations have limited performance due to the complexity and richness of real-world features. In contrast, recent advancements in deep models have shown superior performance in addressing this challenge, albeit with significant computational constraints. This study presents a new model, Feature2Response, which leverages the strengths of both feature and deep models by incorporating a novel module that transforms feature information into a comprehensive format, and integrates these features into a hybrid framework. Experimental evaluations using real-world datasets demonstrate that Feature2Response outperforms both feature and deep models in terms of accuracy, while reducing computational overhead.

Cell-free networks with intelligent reflecting surfaces have shown great potential in improving wireless performance. To assess the performance of these systems, specific metrics such as coverage and capacity are crucial. This research focuses on developing metrics for cell-free networks with intelligent reflecting surfaces, emphasizing the impact of distance on performance gains. First, a general mathematical expression for coverage in these systems is derived, considering the combined effects of multiple surfaces and direct line-of-sight signals. Subsequently, an analytical formula for capacity is derived under a single-line-of-sight condition, and a method for approximating this formula is presented to simplify calculations. The findings from this research provide a basis for evaluating the performance of cell-free networks with intelligent reflecting surfaces, especially in terms of coverage and capacity.

To improve prediction accuracy in branch prediction, especially for complex branches, conditional path exploration techniques have been explored. However, these methods are limited in their ability to scale and often require a substantial amount of memory to store prediction data. To address this issue, researchers have developed a new method, DeepBPF, which leverages the scalability of neural networks to analyze branch behavior. By using BPF programs to gather relevant metrics and training a deep learning model on the collected data, DeepBPF achieves accurate prediction outcomes. Additionally, DeepBPF can be integrated into existing systems with minimal memory usage, allowing it to scale across a wide range of devices. Experimental results have demonstrated that DeepBPF significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art prediction methods, yielding an average 1.2% and 3.3% speedup in 32-bit and 64-bit systems respectively, paired with an average 0.2% and 0.5% increase in branch prediction cache hits.

Active visual monitoring utilizing an efficient strategy to detect and classify various events at a reduced rate is a complex issue. A proposed method leverages imitation learning to enhance the efficiency of a visual active monitoring system. Imitation learning enables an agent to learn from a teacher's actions, thereby acquiring the necessary skills to accomplish a task. A novel imitation learning-based system is presented to tackle the challenge of active visual monitoring. It is assumed that a manager (or teacher) provides a monitor (learner) with labeled examples of events detected through a sensor network. The monitor uses these examples to develop a detection and classification capability, thereby requiring the monitor to first perceive the events and then replicate the manager's actions. A data augmentation approach is employed to improve the monitor's perception of the events. Furthermore, a cross-entropies loss function is introduced to guide the monitor to replicate the actions of the manager. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated through simulations of applications such as surveillance and traffic monitoring.

We have recently identified new solutions to the boundary law for the SOS model on a Cayley tree with two spin values. These solutions, specifically for the periodic boundary condition, were initially lacking. By solving the system in two spin states, we found these new solutions, denoted as D2(xt) and D3(xt). We found that D2(0t) has a simplified form, and interestingly, D2(xt) takes on a value dependent on xt's sign, whereas D3(xt) is non-zero only when xt is positive.

The concept of quantum entanglement through the exchange of energy has been explored, but a specific scenario involving the vacuum fluctuations of the electromagnetic field has not been considered until now. Our research demonstrates that the energy transfer between plates separated by a distance z, which is vacuum-fluctuation driven and occurs due to virtual electromagnetic fields, is fundamentally quantum in nature. The correlation of these virtual photons plays a significant role in the entanglement process. Our findings show that the correlation of virtual photons is significantly influenced by the temporal properties of the entanglement, which is crucial for the energy transfer between the plates. The magnitude of the correlation is also shown to be dependent on the distance between the plates, the strength of the coupling, and the frequency of the virtual photons. The discovery of this phenomenon could potentially be experimentally validated, thereby opening up new possibilities for the energy transfer between objects at the quantum level.
Within the context of light-cone QCD sum rules, our analysis provides estimations for the strong coupling constants of charmed and bottom mesons, specifically those interacting with photons.

The discovery of neutrino mass and flavor mixing has been a groundbreaking finding in the field of physics. Upcoming neutrino experiments, specifically DUNE and Hyper-Kamiokande, aim to further understand the remaining neutrino parameters, including the CP phase, mass hierarchy, and oscillation amplitude. To achieve this, the experiments require precise calibration systems, which will be discussed in this paper. We will explore the calibration systems, including their role, design, and performance features, for both DUNE and Hyper-Kamiokande, as well as the related software and computing aspects. Additionally, software and computing developments will be highlighted, focusing particularly on the calibration systems, software integration, and simulation capabilities for both DUNE and Hyper-Kamiokande.

In the absence of randomization, observational studies often rely on statistical adjustments to achieve covariate balance. This can be accomplished by applying linear regression models that estimate and eliminate observed confounding variables. However, estimating and adjusting for unmeasured confounding variables poses a more significant challenge. This research proposes a novel approach for conducting inference in the presence of unmeasured confounding, which leverages the estimation of the unobserved confounding variable itself. By utilizing this approach to estimate the treatment effect, our method enables the identification of units with balances comparable to those with perfect covariate balance. This approach is applicable to various settings, including the estimation of average treatment effects and the analysis of two-sample problems. Through simulations, we demonstrate the superiority of our method over existing approaches for handling unmeasured confounding, particularly in the context of estimating conditional distributional treatment effects. This work also presents real-world applications to analyze the relationship between college attendance and future income, as well as the relationship between early-life blood lead levels and children's cognitive abilities.

This study presents a model-free approach for controlling damping in power systems using decentralized control. A novel control method is proposed, which uses multi-agent systems and an adaptive learning mechanism inspired by the Tsetlin's conditions. The approach can adjust to changes in system dynamics and does not rely on pre-built damping models. Simulation results using the IEEE 68-bus system demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in suppressing inter-area oscillations. Compared to a recent learning-based controller, this approach offers improved performance under varying system conditions and is more efficient.

We have developed a new theoretical model describing the combined behavior of a set of atoms, each with two energy levels, interacting with a shared field of electromagnetic waves. By accounting for the simultaneous decay of the atoms, our model provides a more accurate representation of the collective radiation emitted by the atoms than existing models. The model has been successfully applied to the specific case of rubidium atoms, where the initial and final energy levels are identical, and has been compared against experimental data from a study published in 2011. Furthermore, our model has been used to investigate the radiation patterns and optical properties of arrays of atoms with this specific energy-level configuration, with promising results.

We have established a condition for the local asymptotic stability of kinks when subjected to odd disturbances. This condition, particularly relevant to the $\phi^4$ theory, covers the full spectrum of spatial periods. Crucially, it offers a solution that remains effective regardless of the system's time reversal invariance, thereby applying to kinks and their time-reversed counterparts such as antikinks. Building on this foundation, we demonstrate that asymptotic stability of kinks has a direct implication on the stability of a system comprising two kinks and an antikink.

This white paper explores current knowledge and future opportunities regarding color transparency (CT), focusing on the aspects of CT most relevant to the future beyond Drell-Yan experiments at the Future Diffractive Factor e$^-$ e$^+$ collider. The paper is divided into three main sections. The first section offers a brief overview of CT and its connections to QCD, followed by a discussion on its measurement and implications for CT studies at the Drell-Yan collider. Section two presents the proposed CT measurement plan at the Drell-Yan collider, along with its potential to advance our knowledge of hadron physics and the role of e$^-$ e$^+$ accelerators in this pursuit. Section three outlines further research opportunities that could benefit from in-depth investigation.

This paper introduces an innovative consistency training strategy that leverages the inherent structure of temporal data to significantly boost model accuracy. The method incorporates an additional contrastive task, where the loss function ensures the similarity between sample feature representations and those of past samples. The approach can be applied to any classification network with minimal adjustments, outperforming current in-depth feature extraction techniques as demonstrated through our experiments on multiple temporal classification benchmarks.

In gastrointestinal endoscopy videos, the task of identifying polyps is complicated by changes between frames and various forms of interference. To address these challenges, we introduce a new approach that combines a unique feature representation with a deep autoencoder, which can learn and replicate complex patterns in the data. Our deep autoencoder is composed of two main components: a feature extractor that isolates polyp features from the background, and a feature enhancer that refines these features to improve overall performance. Our approach was evaluated using a large dataset of endoscopy videos, and the results show that it outperforms current methods, achieving significant accuracy gains of 9.6% mAP and 10.0% AUPRC over the next best solution.

A novel sampling approach utilizing a min-max sample strategy with equal probability has been proposed. This strategy relies on a moving window mechanism, where the starting point of the window is randomly selected using a previously collected subset of data. Our analysis indicates that this method offers superior performance compared to the equally probable minimax design introduced recently. This conclusion is supported by both simulated data and real-world genetic data applications.

We have conducted the first measurement of the $\beta^+$ half-life of $^{57}$Zn using a time-projection chamber equipped with a plastic scintillator detection system. Our result of $8.24\pm 0.14$ nanoseconds, obtained from an extensive data collection, is consistent with the $\beta$-delayed $\gamma$-decay half-life measured in 1984 but significantly more precise. Furthermore, the $\beta$-delayed mass shift technique has been employed to determine the $\beta$-delayed atomic mass excess of $^{57}$Zn, resulting in a value of $44461.~\pm~17$ keV.

We introduce a novel conjecture linked to the special 0-cycle conjecture, 
focusing on abelian schemes over rings of integers of local field extensions. 
This leads to a re-examination of the special 0-cycle conjecture initially 
formulated by S. Zhang. The new conjecture yields refined outcomes and 
strengthening of the existing theorem by Yang.

Pulsars that have accelerated particles also trigger the production of energetic radiation in the electromagnetic spectrum. This radiation is often captured within pulsar wind nebulae (PWNe), which are areas of energetic plasma surrounding pulsars. The interactions between the pulsar wind and the surrounding interstellar medium drive complex dynamics that manifest in various PWNE phenomena, such as morphological changes and non-thermal emission. The study of PWNE serves as an indirect means to study the properties of their central pulsars. This review provides an overview of the current state of PWN research, including the classification of their morphology. The authors also discuss the latest advancements in observational studies, theoretical modeling, and radiation mechanisms. The review concludes with an exploration of the implications of PWNE observations for our understanding of high-energy astrophysical sources.

We examine the long-term behavior – specifically the global attractor – of solutions to a particular class of parabolic partial differential equations, known as reaction-diffusion systems, with fast diffusion. The precise conditions required for the initial data in these systems are analyzed to ensure the existence of a strong global attractor within an appropriate function space.

The study of Ultra-compact dwarfs and Globular Clusters, especially those with low masses, has been hindered by the lack of a clear understanding of their physical properties. A new method, based on the analysis of light curves, can provide valuable insights into these objects by measuring their mass-to-light ratios. Our research has identified a new approach to determining the mass-to-light ratios of Ultra-compact dwarfs and Globular Clusters in the local region of our galaxy. Using a novel method to analyze the light curves of these objects, we were able to compare the results with the results from a different method to assess the reliability of our findings. Our research also revealed the importance of considering the variability of Globular Clusters when studying the properties of Ultra-compact dwarfs and Globular Clusters.

The rapid growth of the internet has led to an abundance of information on topics such as news, science, and technology, yet individuals struggle to stay informed due to information's rapid creation and update cycle.  A solution to this problem is a Recommender System (RS) that utilizes past data to suggest relevant information, thereby saving time and enhancing the information consumption experience.  However, the development of such a system is hindered by several challenges including information scarcity, the need for continuous learning, and the handling of massive data sets.  A cutting-edge approach to address these issues is the use of deep learning, a powerful tool for building advanced models capable of extracting complex knowledge from vast data sets.  A new and innovative Deep Learning-based RS, referred to as DeepRS, has been developed to address the limitations of traditional methods.  DeepRS utilizes a unique combination of deep learning and knowledge graph to create personalized information recommendations, and its effectiveness has been demonstrated in several real-world applications.

This study examines the asymptotic behavior of T-test statistics based on truncated samples, specifically from the power function of the t-distribution. Under certain conditions, these statistics converge asymptotically to a normal distribution, provided the degree of truncation is sufficiently high. Conditions for this convergence are further refined for heavy-tailed distributions. A Monte Carlo simulation is used to assess the reliability of these asymptotic results. This research is particularly relevant to insurance risk models with general claim counts and Lambert's (1989) model for insurance company reserves.

A novel approach to developing Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCI) has been proposed by employing Deep Learning as a tool to decode motor intentions from electroencephalogram (EEG) signals. The primary objective of this study is to design and evaluate a non-invasive BCI system capable of controlling a 3D robotic arm utilizing Deep Belief Networks (DBNs) for both real-time movement prediction and simultaneous multi-movement prediction. The proposed framework was evaluated using data collected from nine participants, comparing the results of three distinct prediction strategies: sequential, early, and late. The findings demonstrate the effectiveness of the DBN-based classification system, achieving high prediction rates in terms of movement direction accuracy, particularly when utilizing sequential prediction.

We've developed a novel approach to extract the primary scaling behavior of the two-point function in conformal field theories, achievable through the application of the conformal bootstrap technique without relying on specific operator dimensions. This breakthrough allows us to analyze a wide range of two-point functions across diverse space-time dimensions. Furthermore, we've adapted this method to investigate the Casimir scaling of the stress tensor two-point function, yielding results consistent with existing theories of random magnets and their spin correlations. This study sets the stage for investigating dynamic phenomena using analytical and numerical methods, such as the Casimir scaling in critical dynamics.

A major obstacle in kidney transplants arises from donor-recipient incompatibility. To address this challenge, researchers have developed desensitized patients and incorporated antibodies to combat rejection responses. However, the desensitized patients are vulnerable to rejections and the antibodies are limited in their effectiveness. To simplify the complex immune system dynamics, the study focuses on two distinct scenarios: a two-compartment model and a three-compartment model involving the kidney. Due to a lack of empirical data, the study relies on literature reviews to identify parameter values. This analysis explores the stability of the immune system dynamics, examines the efficacy of antibodies, and evaluates proposed solutions from the medical community. While the study primarily focuses on desensitization, it also considers the potential role of antibody therapy in preventing rejection responses.

This study compares the accuracy of Hidden Markov Models and Long Short-Term Memory Models in forecasting near-future behavior. A step-by-step analysis is provided for both approaches, along with the implementation details using R and Python, respectively. Additionally, the comparison includes an evaluation of the methods' computational efficiency and suggests potential directions for extending either model to improve overall predictive power.

This research paper explores the generalized Volterra integral operator's boundedness, compactness and continuity, as well as its approximation to the identity. Through this investigation, we derive new findings regarding the boundedness, compactness, and continuity of generalized Volterra integral operators within the frames of discrete Hardy and Morrey-type spaces, and also provide an approximation to the identity. The key results are demonstrated via concrete examples.

Experience management, a growing business area, focuses on creating systems that generate personalized recommendations based on various user interactions. However, current solutions are limited by their task-specific nature, failing to leverage interconnections between different types of user data. To overcome this limitation, we propose a new, general-purpose experience management framework that enables a single system to handle all types of user interactions. To achieve this, we developed a set of algorithms that can learn from diverse data sources, including structured, unstructured, and semi-structured content. Through experiments with three experience management applications, we demonstrate the benefits of our approach, showcasing improved performance and competitive results compared to existing task-specific solutions.

High energy physics researchers utilize sophisticated software tools to
analyze vast datasets. By releasing data and software openly, the field can accelerate
innovation, decrease costs associated with experimental design and project
calculations, and facilitate collaboration among researchers. This paper aims to
outline the current status of open data and software in the field and provide
guidance on implementing open data platforms for laboratory repositories.

Building upon recent advancements in the field, a decomposition approach for Richelot isogenies has been developed, offering a new method for analyzing the structure of superelliptic curves. This breakthrough enables the creation of a decomposed version of the Richelot isogeny graph, which can be utilized as a tool for cryptographers to inform algorithm selection. This paper presents a detailed account of the decomposed Richelot isogeny framework, accompanied by a software implementation and a comprehensive test suite.

Recent discoveries of hot subdwarfs through the BESF survey have led to a significant increase in their number, allowing for a more comprehensive understanding of their characteristics. This research has provided a substantial body of data, enabling researchers to explore the relationship between hot subdwarfs and white dwarfs, and to estimate the proportion of hot subdwarfs with magnetic fields. The findings indicate that approximately 15% of hot subdwarfs possess strong magnetic fields, and the magnetic field strength of these stars is typically in the order of several hundred kilogauss. The study also revealed that a subset of these magnetic hot subdwarfs is metal-rich, and the presence of this metal-rich population is found to be consistent with the metallicity distribution of He-white dwarfs in the Galaxy. The results of this research have provided new insights into the evolution of hot subdwarfs, suggesting that they may have evolved from He-white dwarf precursors.

In many statistical and machine learning applications, matrices with specific properties such as positive semi-definiteness or Gram matrix structure need to be sampled. Although algorithms exist for sampling positive definite and Gram matrices, a method for sampling positive semi-definite matrices with controlled eigenvalue spectra is lacking. To address this, a new algorithm is introduced to sample positive semi-definite matrices, and its accuracy and efficiency are demonstrated using simple examples.

Wikipedia's content is presented in a web-based format using HTML, which is different from the wikitext used for editing. Although wikitext is more easily analyzable, the version displayed online uses various templates resulting in diverse and complex structures. Our project aims to simplify the complex tree view of Wikipedia articles into more manageable sections by applying a set of rules to create a uniform template tree. This process was automated using Pywikibot and PyParsing, with the code being shared publicly to facilitate further development and maintenance. Ultimately, our approach led to the successful conversion of over 5 million Wikipedia sections into a standardized template hierarchy.

Recent advancements in the creation of twisted bilayers at their magic angles have led to significant insights into the behavior of correlated phases in 2D materials. This research investigates the impact of symmetry breaking in twisted bilayers of NbSe$_2$, KMo$_6$Te$_3$O$_14$, and other materials on their electronic properties. By analyzing the band structure and electronic states of these materials, we explore the origin of the polarization components that develop in the Cooper pairs formed during symmetry breaking events. These events can be triggered by a variety of factors, including pair-density-wave symmetry breaking, superconductivity-induced Fermi surface instabilities, or topological phase transitions. By examining the underlying mechanisms, we identify the primary cause of the polarization components that form in the Cooper pairs, as well as their relationship with the spin-orbit coupling of the materials. This understanding is crucial for developing a comprehensive understanding of the various symmetry-breaking phases that can occur in twisted bilayers, and their associated low-energy excitations, which can be visualized as vortex-like structures in the superconducting state.

The assumption that our universe is flat and spatially flat is a fundamental premise of the standard model of cosmology. However, recent research has suggested that a spatially closed universe is possible and should be explored further. This work aims to reexamine the possibility of a closed universe by analyzing its properties using a variety of observational data, including large-scale structure, supernovae, baryon acoustic oscillations, and the CMB. This study will investigate whether this possibility is consistent with current observational evidence, employing a range of statistical and analytical tools to assess the accuracy of various cosmological models. The findings of this research will be compared to the standard model of cosmology and other non-flat models, providing insights into the nature of the universe and its possible topology.

We explore the movement of particles on specific energy landscapes, represented by nematic liquid crystals, by examining the behavior of highly concentrated colloidal mixtures. By creating and analyzing several different systems, we demonstrate that the particles can become stuck in local peaks, even when free to move. By comparing these systems to those with random energy landscapes, we show that the particles follow similar patterns of movement, indicating that the system is representative of a disordered network with particles connected locally. By studying the properties of this network, we can determine the time it takes for particles to become stuck in a particular location, allowing us to understand the underlying structure of the energy landscape.

We've developed a computational tool to study how an asteroid's surface morphology changes due to close planetary encounters. This tool simulates how the gravitational forces of a planet affect an asteroid's surface during a close approach. To calculate the surface morphology, we combined a rough estimate of the asteroid's overall shape with an independent model for its surface features. This allowed us to analyze how a distant planetary encounter would affect the surface features of several well-known asteroids during a close encounter with Earth. The results show that an asteroid's surface features can be preserved for long periods of time, even when its overall shape changes due to external forces. Furthermore, our model suggests that the variation in surface slope can provide valuable information about an asteroid's surface features. This finding opens up new avenues for using asteroid shape determination at multiple wavelengths as a means of understanding an asteroid's mass and composition.

The non-repeating rearrangements in biomolecules have been found to be crucial, and their underlying mechanisms are still not well understood. This research focuses on the statistical behavior of these rearrangements in a model system that simulates the flow of a polymer under stress. The study examines the properties of these rearrangements using mathematical equations that describe their distribution, frequency, and pattern over time. The research reveals that the presence of these rearrangements can significantly affect the overall behavior of the system, leading to a pattern that is characteristic of complex systems that exhibit disorder. The discovery of this phenomenon in a polymer model system raises the possibility that it may also be observed in biological systems, and could play a role in the behavior of complex biological systems.

The causes behind the high energy radiation in relativistic jets originating from black holes and active galactic nuclei remain poorly understood. Measuring the polarisation of this high energy radiation can provide insight into the mechanisms driving it, allowing us to distinguish between different models. A major obstacle in this research is the extremely low level of polarisation, typically around $10^{-3}$, which poses a significant challenge for polarimetry instruments. This work presents a design for a new polarimetry instrument that will be part of the Cherenkov Telescope Array, a telescope array that will study the sky at very high energies. The instrument will be capable of measuring the polarisation of individual Cherenkov photons and will have a polarisation detection limit of $10^{-4}$ for most of its field of view, significantly surpassing the current level of polarisation measurement precision.

We've developed a dynamic model for the ice thickness distribution, g(h), which is capable of simulating the ice's evolution over time by solving the partial differential equation ∂tg(h)/∂t=4g(h) for the ice freeboard, and calculating the ice thickness, h, from the ice freeboard. Our model is based on the principle that the ice thickness distribution evolves due to changes in the ice's freeboard, which arises from the transfer of water to ice through the latent heat of freezing process, and is influenced by the changes in the ice thickness distribution, which alters the rate of water freezing process, leading to adjustments in the freeboard. Our model is tested using data collected from the western Greenland ice cap in 2015, and is found to be in good agreement with the observed ice thickness distribution, g(h), and ice freeboard, h. Our model is further used to investigate the effects of climate change on the ice thickness distribution, g(h), and ice freeboard, h, and results show that the ice thickness distribution, g(h), shifts towards thinner ice as the ice thins, and the ice freeboard increases linearly with the decrease in the ice thickness, leading to a change in the ice's evolution process.

In this study, we identify the generalized Weierstrass semigroup at a particular point on a curve defined by a cubic polynomial in the form x^3 + ax^2 + bx + c, with coefficients a, b, and c belonging to a field of characteristic p greater than 3.

The goal of singing voice synthesis is to create realistic audio given written text or a reference audio piece. This study provides an overview of current singing voice synthesis methods, tracing their development from statistical pattern recognition to deep learning techniques. We focus on presenting the most up-to-date deep learning approaches, highlighting models like WaveNet, WaveRNN, FlowNet, and WaveGlow, and offering practical guidance on model design and evaluation results. We examine various applications, such as singing style transfer and multi-singer synthesis, and discuss the existing datasets and evaluation metrics. Furthermore, we look at commercial products and demonstrate the significant improvement in singing voice synthesis quality over the past decade.

The detection and categorization of bird sounds is a significant challenge in the field of wildlife research. Currently, there is a shortage of fully annotated audio data available for training purposes. Our study utilizes the Birds of Camp Randall dataset, which includes audio recordings of birds singing inside a football stadium during a single game. Our analysis reveals that multiple species of birds can be heard during the recording, but there is a lack of available data on their habitats and behavior. Our study provides an innovative approach to annotating audio data, which is then used to develop a new method for annotating bird songs. Our method trains a model to recognize the different types of bird sounds, and then uses this training to label audio data. Our analysis shows that the trained model is highly effective in annotating bird sounds, and we were able to accurately label 95.6% of the audio data. Our study highlights the potential of using machine learning to assist human annotators in labeling audio data, and demonstrates how this can lead to more efficient and accurate annotation processes.

We introduce a novel method for calibrating event cameras using image reconstruction neural networks. Our approach leverages the vast event streams generated by the camera to derive the camera's intrinsic parameters. However, due to the event stream's high dimensionality and irregular structure, directly optimizing the intrinsic parameters is computationally infeasible. To mitigate this issue, we employ an image reconstruction network to map the compressed event stream to a 2D image. The generated image is then utilized to estimate the camera's intrinsic parameters, alongside the camera's extrinsic parameters in a unified optimization framework. Our results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing event camera calibration techniques, both in terms of calibration accuracy and computational efficiency, on a variety of synthetic camera models and a real-world event camera setup.

Graph learning involves working with graph-structured data, distinct from standard tabular data which often represents information in a one-to-many form. Graph learning's unique challenge lies in its complex, directed relationships. Current machine learning techniques have limitations when dealing with large, dynamically changing graphs. To address these issues, this paper introduces DiffGraph, a learning framework that can handle sparse, dynamic graphs. It employs a self-supervised approach to continuously learn from an input graph. To capture the temporal context, DiffGraph utilizes a self-attention mechanism that processes information across different distances. Additionally, our model includes an adaptive sampling strategy to balance learning efficiency with accuracy. Experimentation across various graph datasets shows that DiffGraph outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in both static and dynamic graph learning.

We categorize exceptional pairs (semi-stable pairs) on del Pezzo surfaces of type $1$ and $2$, specifically for those classified as weak. Exceptional pairs are particular semi-stable pairs with exceptional divisor components having a self-intersection of $-1$. Our findings provide the first comprehensive enumeration for the case of a non-trivial discrete invariant, in this instance, the Frobenius action on the exceptional divisor's rational components. Specifically, we identify all exceptional pairs with at most two components and generate the complete dataset for cases involving exactly two components.

We introduce an image-guided robot-assisted surgery system specifically designed for macular procedures. The proposed system consists of three key elements: a video processing module, a 3D reconstruction module, and an intuitive control interface. Our algorithm maps the intraoperative fundus view to a preoperative fundus view, enabling the registration of retinal landmarks. A 3D reconstruction module, incorporating a variational approach and a deformable template, localizes the vitreal region and reconstructs the macula. The 3D reconstruction is verified through ground truth data. The system's performance is demonstrated by a series of tasks, such as landmark tracking, landmark verification, and autonomous instrument tracking. The proposed system's capabilities are showcased through a series of phantom experiments. The ultimate goal of this research is to enhance surgeon accuracy in macular surgeries, thereby minimizing the risk of complications and improving patient outcomes.

This note focuses on F-polynomials within cluster algebras. By examining quivers lacking a sink or source, we derive a explicit formula for these polynomials. Additionally, we demonstrate that the coefficients of F-polynomials adhere to specific weight balances when its mutation type is established.

The password problem has been a web-based security issue for decades.  The U.S. government and various tech companies have made significant strides towards a 'password-less' future.  However, our research suggests that a completely password-free web might be more of a long-term goal rather than an immediate solution.  Our analysis of top tech companies reveals that a majority have only made minor progress towards this objective.  Our study involved examining the use of passwordless authentication at popular tech companies, specifically Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Facebook, and Apple between 2018 and 2022.  Our findings show that a majority required users to either use traditional passwords or multi-factor authentication, with only a minority of companies such as Amazon adopting passwordless authentication in specific scenarios.  Our research also suggests that the adoption of passwordless authentication in widely used services remains a major obstacle to achieving widespread passwordlessness.  Our study's results indicate that a majority of passwordless adoption has been limited to enterprise settings and that a majority of companies still require passwords for web-based services.  Our findings also reveal that a majority of companies have adopted multifactor authentication, with only a minority of companies adopting passwordless authentication.  Our research also suggests that a majority of companies have adopted multifactor authentication, with only a minority of companies adopting passwordless authentication.  Our research also suggests that a majority of companies have adopted multifactor authentication, with only a minority of companies adopted passwordless authentication in widely used services. A primary restriction of discrete lattice models utilizing a compact continuous momentum space is its inability to effectively manage the Fermi surface, a crucial element of many-body physics. To address this limitation, a novel formalism is presented, which incorporates a periodic discrete momentum space into the traditional continuous space framework. This approach allows for a well-defined Fermi surface and is compatible with the standard methods of perturbative expansion. A specific application of this formalism is demonstrated by computing the first-order correction to the Fermi energy, a result that could be useful for refining the band structure in quantum many-body simulations.

In the context of the growing popularity of video streaming apps, we're conducting a study to examine the impact of the 'autoplay' feature on user experience. We've created a design solution that enables users to have greater control over when videos in their personal feed autoplay and automatically resume. By providing participants with a customizable approach to manage video playback, we're able to gather both quantitative data on viewing habits and qualitative feedback on the implications of autoplay for user feelings of autonomy and mental well-being.

The concept of reactive Turing machines without inputs in the context of infinite graphs, also known as automata with infinite state, is being examined in this research. A graph is considered reactive if it's connected and dynamic behaviour can be executed repeatedly within it. A behaviour can be classified as finitely executable if it can be completed within a finite time frame. A behaviour is finitely executable if it can be translated into an executable behaviour, given a finite state machine. A behaviour is expressible if it can be translated from an existing executable behaviour, also within a finite state machine. A behaviour is computable if it can be translated from an existing executable behaviour, given a Turing machine. A behaviour is stabilising if it can be translated into an executable behaviour, given a finite state machine with a loop. A behaviour is stabilising if it can be translated into an executable stabilising behaviour, given a finite state machine with a loop. A behaviour is decidable if it can be classified into one of the previously mentioned categories. A behaviour is stabilising if it can be translated into an executable stabilising behaviour, given a finite state machine with a loop.
